extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, policy researchers, agency staff, regulated parties, and empirical regulatory analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Measuring how discrete regulatory obligations (sentence-level deontic instructions) change between proposed and final rules by extracting, structuring, pairing, and comparing obligations from Federal Register proposals and final rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each obligation is defined as a discrete deontic instruction directed at an actor — for example, 'the operator MUST inspect the equipment' or 'no person MAY enter the facility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations are the clauses or sentences that tell a regulated person or entity what they must, must not, or may do; these discrete commands are treated as the impactful elements of a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: obligation-level (not document-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: The impactful element of a rule is not the document itself but the discrete instructions (obligations) it contains; analyses should operate at the obligation/clause/sentence level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measuring change at the obligation level (rather than at the level of entire regulations or documents) reveals transformations that document-level comparisons can obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-level extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Extract obligations at the sentence level from Federal Register rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sentence delimitation so each extracted unit corresponds to a discrete deontic instruction; this supports downstream structuring and matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation structure: actor, modal verb, action, object
rubrics_metrics.description: Each extracted sentence-obligation is separated and structured into four components: the actor, the modal verb, the action, and the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structuring obligations into these components facilitates deterministic filtering, matching across versions, and analysis of changes (including deontic changes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterministic and reproducible filtering mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a deterministic, reproducible filtering process to separate and structure sentence-level obligations from the rule text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reproducible filter enables large-scale, transparent extraction and comparison; it underpins claims about survival rates and other metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing proposed and final rules using metadata (docket identifiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed rules should be paired with their corresponding final rules using metadata such as docket identifiers to allow direct obligation-level comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate pairing (e.g., via docket ids) is required to create obligation sets for each version and to perform redline-style comparisons at scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation survival rate (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of proposed obligations that survive into the final rule in syntactically recognizable form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported example: across 954 paired proposed-to-final comparisons, about 32% of proposed obligations survive in syntactically recognizable form; this measures structural persistence rather than semantic continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net obligation flow
rubrics_metrics.description: A metric capturing the net inflow/outflow of obligations between proposed and final rules (i.e., how many obligations are removed versus added or modified).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to quantify asymmetries such as more proposed obligations being removed than modified; example counts: ~13,700 proposed obligations disappeared, ~2,050 appeared as modified versions, and ~6,700 obligations were introduced in final rules with no proposal antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deontic drift rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The rate at which surviving obligations change their modal 'force' (e.g., from 'must' to 'may' or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported example: a deontic drift rate of roughly 0.6%, meaning fewer than one percent of surviving obligations change their modal characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survival classification categories (survive, removed, modified, added)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify each proposed obligation as surviving unchanged (matched syntactically), removed entirely, appearing as a modified version of a counterpart, or final-rule-only (added).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The matching method places obligations into these categories; many edited obligations appear in the 'modified' category, while removals dominate overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching method: syntactic recognizability (structural persistence) vs semantic continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Match obligations across versions based on syntactic/structural similarity; acknowledge that syntactic non-survival does not necessarily imply semantic disappearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The survival measure examines structural persistence rather than meaning; agencies may preserve underlying obligations conceptually even when wording changes enough to fail syntactic matching. This distinction is a central caveat for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching tolerance for textual change
rubrics_metrics.description: The matching approach tolerates significant textual change before classifying an obligation as non-matching; many edited obligations qualify as 'modified' rather than 'removed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matching thresholds should be selected and reported; even with substantial tolerance, a large share of proposed obligations can still be classified as non-surviving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpus scope and sample size requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify the corpus and timeframe used for extraction and comparison (e.g., Federal Register documents spanning 2016–2026; more than 520,000 documents; hundreds of thousands of obligations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting corpus size and number of paired comparisons (example: 954 paired proposed-to-final comparisons) is necessary to contextualize metrics and their generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-agency variance as an analytic dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare survival and other metrics across agencies because stability varies dramatically by agency and regulatory domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Treasury regulations show ~57% survival, Interior ~19%; possible explanatory factors include technical complexity, stakeholder involvement, political visibility, and internal drafting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive caveat: legal/functional consequences of syntactic change
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when an agency intends to preserve meaning, substantial syntactic rewriting can have functional or legal consequences because administrative law often depends on close textual readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should note that syntactic non-survival may affect how regulated parties or courts treat provisions, so structural measurements may understate practical impact on regulated behavior and litigation outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic framing: notice-and-comment as filter versus incremental editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use obligation-level metrics to evaluate whether the notice-and-comment process functions primarily as a line-by-line editing process or as a selection/filtering mechanism that narrows a broader universe of proposed obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The observed pattern (e.g., low survival rate, many removals, and many final-rule-only additions) supports framing notice-and-comment more as a selection process; this framing has implications for how stakeholders prioritize commenting resources and for empirical scrutiny of the 'notice' element.
